block-definition.comment: SENTENCE is the main constructor for sentences, represented as lists of words. It takes zero or more inputs, each of which can be either a list or a text string. If a list, the input is assumed to be a list of words. If a text string, it is converted to a list of words using SENTENCE→LIST. Then all the lists of words are appended to form a new list of words. If the inputs are lists of lists rather than lists of words, SENTENCE, like APPEND, does only one level of flattening, reporting a list of all the items of all the input lists.
Takes a (possibly deep) list as input, and reports a human-readable text form of the list (namely, Lisp notation).

scripts.comment: In PLURAL, it's important that the test for words with irregular plurals comes first! Otherwise, if the irregular word ends with a letter we test for, that test will succeed and PLURAL will report the regular form. This is an important general rule: In a sequence of tests, make the /most specific/ test first.

How can that work? PLURAL-SPACE removes only one space! The students don't yet know that since PLURAL calls PLURAL-SPACE, and PLURAL-SPACE calls PLURAL, this is an example of mutual recursion. This TIF is an early hint about recursion. It is *not* the main presentation of recursion, and it's not important if students don't get the idea at this point. In particular, don't feel the urge to load this example with the whole apparatus of base cases and so on. In fact, you don't have to introduce the word "recursion" unless students ask for it. ("Is there a name for this?") The serious presentation of recursion comes in Unit 7, after the AP Exam. Assure the students that the answer to TIF D (as for all TIFs) won't be on that exam.

To make this work, you have to modify LONGEST TRAILING SUBSTRING to go through its loop length+1 times:

The /really/ best students may be frustrated by the lack of explanation of some bits of magic, especially the need to unringify the call to ITEM 2 OF in PLURAL. The best way to explain it is to have them try ringifying it! The result will be that PLURAL reports the second item of the key-value pair, namely, a ringified block. It's that block, not ITEM, that we want CALL to call. So by unringifying the ITEM 2 OF block, we let Snap! evaluate it, finding the ringified block from the pair, and /that/ becomes the first input to CALL. If that's not enough of an explanation, send them to Chapter VI of the Snap! Reference Manual.
